column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

Birth: the article gives 10 February 1830 (c.); the entry's dates say c. 1831. Birth year left out of the text. The article calls the 1910 march an advance north of Tiznit against Sultan Abdelhafid; the entry says a failed march on Fez. Worded without naming Fez.

The article gives three possible birth dates (12 December 1699, 16 December 1705 or 1 January 1718); the entry gives 1718. Birth left out. The entry says he died in Bangkok; the article places Taksin's court at Thonburi. The place of death is left unnamed. The literary society in the entry is not in the article.

The article says Ei-hime was six at the marriage of 1581 but gives her birth as 1574; her age is left out. The entry says he received lands after 1600 making the Maeda the wealthiest daimyo family; the article gives 1,025,000 koku, second only to the shogun, which agrees.

The article dates his life c. 558 to 31 January 632; the entry says fl. c. 600 and died in the early 7th century, which agree. The exact death date is left out since the article itself mentions two dates of death. The entry says he founded Ferns around 600; the article places the grant after the battle of 598.

Rankings section left out by rule. The library section says approximately 3,500 books are preserved in a collection and 6,31,735 volumes in all; only the volume count used. The entry mentions the faculty of fine arts; the article as given has no section on it, so it is not described. Founding: article gives 30 April 1949 as the day it became a public university; entry says 1949.

The entry says the city is usually identified with Maheshwar; the article presents Mandhata and Maheshwar as the two main proposals without saying which is usual. The text gives both without ranking them. Baahubali in popular culture left out.
SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, mostly geography already in the description; too little for a longer text
SKIPPED: article has under 400 words, much of it travel distances and a confused lead (dates 8th-12th century against the entry's 7th-12th); not enough for 260 words without padding
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words of substance (exile, rebellion, a treaty and a letter); too little for 260 words without padding

The entry says the Maniots resisted Ottoman control throughout Ottoman rule; the article does not state this directly. Not repeated. Genetic study claims kept attributed to the studies; the 2017 study's suggestion of Dorian descent left out as speculative.
Article lead says KiHa 183 trains from JR Hokkaido run from 3 September 2025; the 21st-century section says traffic restarted 5 September 2025. Worded as September 2025.

The article says he planned for Shogun Tokugawa Ieshige to move to Kyoto in 1862; Ieshige was an 18th-century shogun, so this is a slip. Left out. The article lists the Four Wise Lords once with Shimazu Nariakira, Date Munenari and Yamauchi Yōdō, and once with Yamauchi Toyonobu; only the group name used.

Much of the article's Origins section rests on oral tradition and royal genealogy without dates; it is attributed to tradition in the text. The article says a present king reigns at Lumbala Nguimbo; left out as present-day. Third section paragraph is near the upper length; check.
Article gives Nabopolassar's coronation as 22/23 November 626 BCE; written as November 626 BCE. Article dates the megadrought 675-550 BCE; dates left out to keep the paragraph short.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words of anecdote (Helmarshausen dispute, Haimerad, a joke about his Latin); too little for 260 words without padding

The entry dates it around 1131-1143. The article says it must be after 1131 and could be any time before Melisende's death in 1161, and that palaeographical comparisons suggest the 1140s or even 1150s. The palaeographic dating is left out so as not to contradict the entry's range. The entry says it was made in the scriptorium of the Holy Sepulchre; the article agrees. Crusader Kings III in popular culture left out.

The entry calls Milcom the national god of the Ammonites; the article says he was either the national god or an important god, and that some scholars (Walter Aufrecht) think he was only the god of the royal house. That doubt is left out so as not to contradict the entry. The entry's Solomon shrine and Josiah's destruction are not described in the article beyond the verse references; not repeated.

Death: the article gives 23 February 727; the entry says d. c. 715. The year is left out. The entry calls her the first abbess; the article says the house was first directed by a French abbess, Liobinde of Chelles, whom Mildburh succeeded. Her place in the succession is left out. The entry dates the foundation around 680; the article gives no date. Not repeated.

Birth: the article gives 1329 (and says he died at 37); the entry gives 1331. Birth year and age at death are left out. The entry's statement that his rule was remembered as mild is not in the article. The article's biography says Xu Shouhui appointed 'Xu' as Grand Marshal, an apparent slip for Ming; left out.

The record as the largest pile of bricks and the bell's rank among ringing bells are left out as rankings. The article says Mingun is about 10 km northwest of Mandalay in Sagaing Region; the entry says north of Mandalay on the west bank, which agrees.

Article says Miraj was 'founded in the early 10th century' but also that the Shilaharas took it at the end of the 9th century; founding date left out. Article dates the Bahmani takeover confusingly (1318, then the town renamed 1347, then 'In 1395 the Bahmanis conquered Miraj'); only the Hasan Gangu account and the 1347 renaming kept. Article gives Ibrahim Adil Shah I's reign as 1534-1558 but his death as 1580; the death year left out. Article: Santaji Ghorpade Deshmukh of Miraj in 1680, Aurangzeb took it six years later, yet Bijapur fell to the Mughals in 1687; left out. Entry says Sangli broke away in 1782; the article does not mention this. Not used.

Entry calls Mirgissa 'probably' the Iken of Egyptian texts; the article says the Hathor stele 'enabled positive identification'. Kept only the stele naming Hathor mistress of Iken, without stating certainty. Entry names the lake Lake Nasser; the article Lake Nubia (the Sudanese part of the same reservoir). Lake not named. Article says Vercoutter excavated 'without Sudanese permission'; left out as not needed.

Entry: died c. 1199, prince from the 1160s. Article: prince 1162-1190, died 1198, and also son Toljen succeeding 'ca 1192-1196'. Death year and end of rule left out. Article says he was 'born in the second half of the 12th century', impossible if he ruled from 1162; left out. Entry says he fought the Bosnian ban; the article only says he married Ban Kulin's sister. Not used. Article dates the war with Dubrovnik to both 1184 and 1185; the text gives the 1184 defeat and the 1186 peace only.

Entry says the monastery is documented from the early eleventh century; the article says it dates from the eighth century and is first attested in a 958 document. Both foundation dates left out. Entry calls it a Benedictine abbey (present tense); the article a former Benedictine monastery. Text avoids saying whether monks live there.

Entry calls Mont Blanc the highest mountain of the Alps; the article says of Western Europe. Not repeated. Article names the French commander 'General Moutesquiou' (a misspelling of Montesquiou); name left out. Entry dates the return 1814-1815; the article says it stayed French under the 1814 treaty and was returned under the 1815 treaty. Text follows the article's detail, which fits within the entry's range.
Article calls Margaret of Anjou 'wife of Henry IV' (she was Henry VI's wife); her husband left unnamed. The 'Tudor hall' plans and banknote depictions left out as minor.

Entry says the mine produced until the 1980s; the article says it finally closed in November 1990 (and that the replacement railway closed in 1987). Closure date left out. Entry says gold was found in the early 1880s; article says the town was founded as a gold mining town in 1882 - consistent.
Article: according to legend Bellelay Abbey was founded as a dependency in 1136, which it calls unlikely; left out.

Article gives his dates as 1301-1363 but says in the text that he died in 1364; the entry has d. 1363. Death year left out. Entry says he was deposed and blinded by his sons; the article names only his son Shah Shuja. Text names Shah Shuja without saying he acted alone. Article says Jani Beg 'sent an offer to become his vassal' (ambiguous); worded as an offer to take him as a vassal, which he declined.

Article says Murcia was semi-independent 'since 1244' in the aftermath but surrendered on 2 April 1243 in the background; only the 1243 surrender used. Treaty date disputed in the article (Royal Chronicle 1265, Ibn Idhari 665 AH, O'Callaghan 1267, Doubleday 1266); given as 'from 1265 to 1267'.

Entry dates the temples to about the 9th-11th centuries; the article to between the late eighth and early eleventh centuries. No dating given in the text. Article says Mukhalingam was the Eastern Ganga capital 'from the 6th to the 12th century'; entry calls it the dynasty's early capital. Start date left out; only the 1122 move kept. Article spells the old name Kalinganagari, the entry Kalinganagara; name not repeated.

Article reports necrophilia after Empress Fu's death; left out as lurid and not needed. Entry says Murong Xi was killed by Feng Ba and Gao Yun; the article says Murong Yun (Gao Yun) beheaded him after Feng Ba's rising - consistent.

Article's lead says he succeeded in 1810, its text 'c. 1810'; written as 'around 1810'. Entry says the Bushati family had ruled northern Albania almost independently since 1757; the article does not say this. Not used.

Entry says he ruled in western India; the article says northern India (and Avanti/Malava in present-day Madhya Pradesh). Region of India not named. Entry dates the Arab repulse to around 738; the article gives no year. No year given.

Article says the Dutch ship Breskens reached Nanbu territory 'in the late 16th century', a date that looks doubtful for a Dutch ship in Japan; left out. Article's lead says the Nanbu 'ruled most of northeastern Honshu for over 700 years'; not used.

The article is strongly partisan (an age of 'aggressive imperialism', 'one of the most powerful Hindu rulers', no Muslim invasion for a hundred or for 250 years); none of these judgements used, and the campaign told from the named sources. Article (Gangavashanucharitam) says he ruled 27 years; the entry's 1238-1264 is 26. Length of reign not given. Article spells the brother-in-law Paramadrideva and Paramardi Dev; the second form used. Article gives the governor as 'lkhtiyar-ud-Din Yuzbak' (lower-case L); the governor is left unnamed.

Entry names the Sinhalese prince Manavanna; the article Manavarman. Article form used once - editor may prefer to drop the name. Article says Manavarman ruled Sri Lanka 691-726, which does not fit a reign ending 668; left out. Article garbled sentence calls him a follower and patron of Jainism; left out. Also left out the Culavamsa 'same-sex relationship' claim and the legend of Paranjothi sacrificing his child. Entry gives the title as Vatapikonda, the article Vatapikondan; not repeated.

Article's Luce theory dates the killing to 1165, before the 1167 accession given by both article and entry; year left out. Entry says the Dhammayangyi was left unfinished; the article only says he built it. Completion not mentioned. Entry calls the father Alaungsithu; the article calls him both Alaungsithu and Sithu I. Sithu I used with Alaungsithu implied by the entry.

Entry calls the master a sculptor and architect; the article only a stone sculptor (though it credits innovations in architecture). Not contradicted. Short article: two sections only, about 270 words.
Entry says the NHM held the Cultivation System monopoly; the article does not mention this. Not used.

The article's lead says the resolution was passed on 7 July 1898; its Passage section says it was approved on 6 July and signed on 7 July. The text gives only the signing on 7 July. Group names spelled as the article spells them (Hui Aloha 'Aina, Hui Kulai'aina).

The article says the Basic Records ran to the creation of the Lê dynasty 'in 1482', evidently a slip for 1428; the year is left out. The entry says he compiled the work at Lê Thánh Tông's command; the article says he wrote his own version after the emperor's order for an official chronicle. Worded so as not to contradict the entry.

The article calls Ngwenya 'the world's oldest' and 'the oldest known mine'; the entry says 'one of the oldest known mines'. The superlative is left out and only the dates are given. Left out: the reported corruption over Salgaocar's licence (a donation to the king) and the 2018 announcement of renewed prospecting.

The entry says the Circars were granted to the Company by the Nizam in 1766. The article says a treaty of alliance with Nizam Ali Khan was signed on 12 November 1766 and that by a second treaty, the Treaty of Masulipatnam of 1 March 1768, the Nizam resigned the Circars to the Company. The year of the Nizam's cession is left out. The entry dates the grant to the French to 1753; the article gives no year.

The article says that in Hokkaido Okhotsk remains are absent after 800 BP (about 1100 CE), and that in the Kurils radiocarbon dates decline sharply around 1100 CE; elsewhere it dates the late stage to the 10th to 13th centuries. The entry dates the culture to c. 5th–13th centuries. The 1100 CE figures are left out.
The slur in the original lyrics is not printed; the text refers to it as the offensive word for Black people, as the article's 'less offensive' wording implies.
The entry counts 1,554 songs; the article counts 1,553 poems, of which 1,144 are unique. No count is given in the text.

DISAGREEMENT: the entry says 'the Dutch lost a naval clash in the Arafura Sea'. The article says the opposite: in the Battle of Arafura Sea on 15 January 1962 three Dutch destroyers intercepted four Indonesian motor torpedo boats, sank one, and killed many, among them Commodore Yos Sudarso; some 55 survivors were captured. The battle is left out of the text; the entry's sentence looks wrong and should be checked. The article's lead calls it a combined Soviet–Indonesian operation; left out.

The entry dates the family's rule in Syunik from the 13th century; the article says Elikum I continued the Armenian branch in Syunik and was killed in 1184. That date is left out. The article dates Ivane Orbeli's rebellion 1177-1178 and his killing to 1177.
The article says British sources recorded '8000 out of the estimated 1500 Fante at Anomabu' slain in 1807, an evident slip; no figure is given.

The article gives his dates as 1558 – 1605 in its lead but says in its Death section that he died on 2 September 1610; the entry has 1610. The year of death is left out. The entry says Hideyoshi stripped him of his lands in 1593; the article tells the Pyongyang episode under 1592 without dating the confiscation. No year given for it.

The article's summary says he died 'in September of the same year' (1660); its lead and Later years section give 19 December 1660, as used here. The article calls him '22-year-old Gjedde' when the fleet sailed in 1618, which does not fit a birth in December 1594; his age is left out.

The entry says the pact freed slaves and Chinese indentured workers who had fought with the rebels; the article says it offered manumission to slaves and Chinese immigrants who had fought on either side. The point is left out of the text. The article lists Antonio Maceo among those released under the amnesty, though he rejected the pact; he is left out of that list. The article spells the party 'Partido Liberal Automista' (a slip for Autonomista); its name is not printed.
The article calls Suyurghatmish both a sibling and a half-brother; both are used where the article uses them.

The entry has him the effective ruler from the late 1480s; the article describes his rise through the guard (1495) and his brother's offices (1497) and says he ruled as absolute tyrant once his enemies were removed in 1500. No date is given for the start of his rule. The article says he handed Siena to Borghese 'later that year' (1512) and died 'shortly afterwards', yet dates his death 21 May 1512.

The article dates the move of the capital to 1450 (to Lakhnauti in the lead, to Gaur in the History section) and also says Pandua was capital for 114 years, 1339–1453. The entry says only that the court returned to Gaur in the 15th century; no year is given. The article's 1339 start of the capital does not fit its own 1352 founding of the sultanate; left out.

The article gives his reign as 437 BC to 367 BC; the entry dates him to the 4th century BCE and says he founded Anuradhapura around 437 BCE. No years are given in the text. The article tells the legend as fact; it is framed as the traditional account.
SKIPPED: article too thin: population figures, airlines, climate, and the 2014 air crash search; nothing on the Kotawaringin Sultanate or the town's history

The article gives the surface area as about 22.6 km2; the entry says about 22 square kilometres, so the figure is not repeated. The saying about rainwater is not attributed to anyone in the article; it is given as a principle, without a speaker.

The article's allegations of ties to Vladimir Putin and of high officials supporting fraud are left out: they are attributed claims, poorly sourced in the article, and not needed here. The Spanish prosecutors' allegation is given as theirs.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, nearly all of it already in the entry's description

Birthplace left out: the article gives Elgueta, Gipuzkoa in the lead and a village in Biscay province under Early life. Day of death left out: the lead gives 2 April 1825, the body says he was mortally wounded on 2 April and died the following day. The entry says only April 1825.
The article dates the armed column to São Salvador to 1694, a year before the reign it gives (1695-1718), and places it after discontent in the early eighteenth century; the year is left out.
SKIPPED: article under 280 words, mostly travel details; too little history to add to the entry

The entry says the river forms most of the boundary between Florida and Alabama; the article says it forms part of the boundary along nearly its own entire length. The text does not say how much of the state border it makes. The article dates Spain's ratification only as a couple of years after 1819; no year is given.
The article spells the antiquarian both Lluyd and Lhuyd; Lhuyd is used.
The article's claim of an ancient Saharan script, and that the Vai, Mende and Kpelle scripts were versions of it, is left out as poorly supported.

The article dates the change from the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves to the Empire of Brazil to 1824 in the lead and 1822 in Consequences; no year is given. The article gives the death toll as 'over 4000 Uruguayans (6% of the entire population)'; rendered as people of the Banda Oriental.
The entry says he returned in 1968; the article says he was pardoned in 1968 and returned to French Polynesia in 1969. The year of his return is left out.
The article's claims that he was recognised as Emperor of Hindustan are left out as unclear and poorly supported.

Deportation figures vary: Wang Zhenping gives 78,000 households and Mark Cartwright 200,000 people; the range given is that of the Chinese and Korean sources the article cites. The article dates the Khitan capture of Liaoyang only as after 918; no year is given in the text.

The entry dates him c. 1258-1306; the article gives his birth as between 21 October 1258 and 12 June 1268. No birth year or the two documents are given in the text. The entry dates the division of the father's lands to 1281; the article gives the father's death as 1281 or 1282, Przemysław as duke from 1282, and the formal division between the brothers in 1290. The year of the father's death is left out.
The article does not mention the kouroi named in the entry; nothing is said of them.
The entry says he fought under Andrew Jackson at New Orleans; the article says some sources place him there and others disagree. New Orleans is left out of the text.

The article says Pyinbya founded Pagan in 849; the entry says he fortified the city then. The text gives the chronicles' founding date, which the entry also calls the traditional founding of Pagan as a walled city.
The article calls him a prince; the entry calls him ruler. The article names the ruler who moved the capital in 426 'Qifu Gangui', apparently Qifu Chipan; written without the name.

Dates: the entry has c. 1575-1610; the article gives his reign as 1575 to 1612 and his death around 1612. No end date is printed. Succession: the article contradicts itself (the eldest son Andriantompokoindrindra passed over for the second son Andrianjaka; later Andrianjaka as the younger son by the first wife, the eldest being by the second wife). Left out. The article once writes 'Radama' for Ralambo in the zebu story, and calls the Betsimisaraka a western coastal people; left out.
The article dates the brick rebuilding to 1744-1751; the entry says around 1746. No range printed.
Some references count him as 4th Earl of Chester. The article says he married Constance in 1188 or 1189; written as 'around the same time' as his knighting.
The entry says he was earl from 1129; the article says he inherited the earldom in 1128 (and dates the abbey's foundation three years later). Neither year printed.

The article says he waited 12 years at Kavani, but dates his proclamation to 1439 and the recapture to 1453; the length of the wait is left out. It also calls Rana Kumbha's successor 'Rana Udai Singh I'; left out.

The entry calls them the colony's first missionaries; the article says the Jesuits had been in Acadia since 1611 and that the Recollects were the first order to establish themselves in Quebec. Not repeated. The article also says the Jesuits only arrived in New France in 1625, and has a garbled sentence about Bishop Hubert annulling vows after 1784; both left out.

The entry dates the movement 1765-1771; the article gives 1766 to 1771 for the uprising, though it dates the Nutbush Address to 1765. No span printed. Regulator numbers at Alamance: 'approximately 2,000 (by some accounts, 6,000)'; written as about 2,000.

Birth: the entry has c. 1259; the article gives 1240, and says he may have been young when he became earl in 1271 and came of age in 1280, which fits the entry better. No birth year printed; 1271 also left out.

The entry places the Uí Fidgenti along the river; the article names the O'Donovans and Uí Chairpre Áebda. Both written as the article has it, without the entry's claim of an eastern boundary. The article is short; two sections.
The Annales Casinenses report that 'Robbertus de Surrento' was blinded and died soon after; the article takes this as possibly him. Hedged as 'possibly blinded'.
The article lists a daughter Anne born 1604, before the February 1605 marriage, and has him sitting for Maldon from 1604; dates of children and the Maldon term left out.

The article says the Nawab demanded '40 rods of gold' (apparently a slip for a payment in lakhs); written without the figure. Macaulay wrote long after the impeachment; the article lumps him with Burke's charges. Kept as 'and later Thomas Macaulay'.
The entry has their defeat by Azai Nagamasa in 1560, which the article does not mention; not repeated. The article places the paper guild in Mino, an odd place for an Ōmi clan; the province left out.

The article spells his name Rosli Dhoby; the entry's spelling is used. The article says he 'successfully defended himself' at trial yet was convicted; left out. His age at the time was disputed (17 or 19); not printed.
The entry names the Treaty of Falaise; the article says only that the castle was surrendered after William I's capture at Alnwick. Two sections: the article gives little on the setting.
The article mentions a new version of the text replacing the old (dated '1970-2026') without details; left out. The New Economic Policy launched in 1971 also left out.

The entry dates the Ahom conquest 1523-24; the article gives 1524 for the annexation. Written without the year of annexation. The 1950 earthquake in the entry is not in the article. Bhismaknagar and Rukmini Nagar are near Roing, in Arunachal Pradesh, so they are not placed at Sadiya.
The article dates the House of Khachen to 821 and gives him the title prince of Arran and Shaki, which some scholars dispute; written as scholars' views.

Foundation of Bangor: the entry says around 558; the article says no later than 552 by the annals, 555 by Ussher and most later writers, 559 by Webb. No date printed. Death: the entry says around 602; the article gives 602 (Tigernach, Chronicon Scotorum) or 597 (Inisfallen). No year printed. Birth: the article gives 510-520; the entry c. 510. No year printed.
The article states plainly that he was Brochwel's son; the entry says 'said in tradition', so the text keeps the hedge. The article gives his death as 640; consistent with the entry's 7th century.

The entry dates the war to 1242; the article to 1242-1243 (Raymond's war with Roger of Foix lasted to January 1243, the truce of Pons 1 August 1243). The text keeps the fighting in 1242 and mentions only the truce in 1243. The article gives the Treaty of Paris both 4 December 1259 and ratifications in February 1259 and Henry's homage on 4 December; the ratification dates were left out. The skirmish at Taillebourg is dated 21 or 22 July; the siege of Saintes began 22 or 23 July. The text gives no day for either.
The article calls his office Prime Minister; the entry chief minister. The text uses prime minister, the same office. Asaf Jah VI and Mir Mahbub Ali Khan are the same Nizam.

SKIPPED: article too thin (under 250 words of substance, much of it a list of children) and it contradicts the entry The entry gives his death as 1778; the article gives his dates as 1705-1782. The article's account of his marriage is confused ('By 1770, his legitimacy was strengthened by marriage ... in November 1766').

The entry says he captured Aleppo in 1024; the article dates the conquest to 1025 (the gate opened on 18 January 1025, the citadel fell on 30 June, he entered it in September) and makes him emir from 1025. The text says only that he besieged the city late in 1024 and gives no year for its fall. The battle of al-Uqhuwana is dated 12 or 25 May 1029; the text gives no day.
The article gives his traditional output both as 16,000 hymns and as 'more than 10,000'; the text gives no total. The surviving hymns are given as '383 (384)' and as 384; the text says 383 or 384.

The article quotes Groslier (1921) and Ponder (1936), who held that the sampot common to both sexes is a modern fashion imported from Siam, against Walker (1955), who pointed to the bas-reliefs. The entry dates the sampot to the Funan era, so the Siamese-import view was left out. The article's 'circa the 900s AD' is given as 'about the 900s'.

The 1817 Slave Return lists Archer as 12 years old, which would put his birth about 1805; the 1832 return says he was 31 at his death, matching the entry's 1801. The age in 1817 was left out. The article says the rising 'spread throughout the entire island'; the entry says it spread across western Jamaica. The text gives no geographical extent. The article says the enslaved believed emancipation had been granted 'by the Queen of India', an apparent slip; the text does not name who.

The article's area figures conflict (2000 m2 given as five acres; 50 acres; 20 hectares; 60 hectares); none are used. The entry says much of the population probably moved to found Monte Albán; the article says only that the site fell under Monte Albán's control. Not a contradiction, but the text does not repeat either claim of migration.

The entry calls the 1762 treaty one with the Dutch colony; the article says with the Dutch Crown. The text says only 'their treaty'. The article says about one third of the Saramaka now live in French Guiana; left out as a present-day figure without a date.

The entry dates his reign from c. 174; the article says his coins run from 172 and that Eupator died between 170 and 172. The text says only 'the early 170s'. The entry also credits him with victories over the Tauri; the article names only the Scythians and Sirachi (the entry's Siraces).

The article's opening gives his death as 28 November 1937, but the rest of it, and the entry, give 28 November 1931; the text follows 1931. The entry calls him a former monk and healer; the article a physician and monk. Consistent.

The entry says he captured Jolo in 1638; the article says that after three months of fighting neither side could claim victory and a truce was agreed. The text gives the attack but not its outcome. The article calls him one of the two greatest Spanish military leaders in the Philippines; left out as praise. The article spells the sultan Qudarat; the entry Kudarat.

Pliny is quoted for the lapis specularis mines both as '100,000 places' and '100,000 steps' around Segóbriga; no figure is used. The article dates the Roman conquest to the beginning of the 2nd century BC in the Celtiberian Wars; left out.

The entry says he launched the jihad in 1818; the article says it was probably continuous from 1810 to 1818, or two events in 1810 and 1818, and that he ruled from 1818. The text gives no starting year. The article gives his son's reign as 1844 to 1852, although Seku Amadu died in 1845; the son's dates are left out. The entry calls the state the Massina Caliphate; the article the Massina Empire.

The entry calls Hilarion 'later metropolitan of Kiev'; the article simply 'the metropolitan of Kiev'. The text names him only as Hilarion. The entry says the sermon praises Yaroslav the Wise as well; the article does not mention Yaroslav.

The saved copy of the article stops before her death; the entry's date (933) is not discussed. Miskawayh's account of the succession is one of two; Arib's version has the vizier hesitating between Ibn al-Mu'tazz and Muhammad ibn al-Mu'tamid before the caliph recovered and named Ja'far himself.
The entry says he submitted to the Qing again in 1677; the article gives no year, only that he did so after his father's death in late 1676. The text gives no year.
No disagreement with the entry. Birth year unknown; the article suggests after 720 as a likely inference only, left out.

The entry names Echizen, Owari and Tōtōmi as the governorships; the article names Echizen and Wakasa (from 1335) and Owari, and does not mention Tōtōmi. Not a contradiction, so Tōtōmi is simply not mentioned. The article's sentence on Ieuji is ambiguous ('son of Shiba Yasuuji who established the clan name'); worded to avoid saying which of the two established it. Article thin (about 350 words); two sections.
No disagreement with the entry. The article is short (about 350 words); the text keeps to the founding story and the shrine.

Entry says 'more than a thousand' slips; the article gives roughly 1155. Consistent. The entry names the tomb's owner as the official Xi; the article does not name him, so he is not mentioned. The entry is typed as a place but the article is about the texts; headings follow the texts.
No disagreement with the entry. The year of Taizong's death is not in the article and is not given. The hand story is in the entry and is not repeated.

No disagreement with the entry. The article dates the Kamrup coin 1357–1359, partly before the entry's accession year 1358, and its timing of the Assamese resistance ('after about five years', then 1362) is unclear; the coin's date and the five years are left out.

The entry says the kingdoms came under Dutch control in the late 19th century; the article dates the surrender agreements with the seven kingdoms to 1904. The year 1904 is left out of the text.
